desc:
You are given an array of distinct integers. Decide whether it can be the preorder traversal (root, then left subtree, then right subtree) of some binary search tree, where every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in its right subtree is larger.

Only the array is given, not the tree: you must decide whether any BST has exactly this preorder.

Example 1

preorder = [5,2,1,3,7,6,8]
Output: true
This is the preorder of [5,2,7,1,3,6,8].

Example 2

preorder = [5,2,6,1,3]
Output: false
After 6 (larger than the root 5) we are in the right subtree of 5, so the later 1 cannot appear.

Example 3

preorder = [4]
Output: true
hints: The first value is the root. In a BST preorder, the values smaller than the root come first (left subtree), then the larger ones (right subtree). Checking this recursively is correct but may be slow on skewed input.

Once you have moved to the right of some value x (you read something larger than x after it), every later value must stay larger than x. So you only need the largest such x seen so far as a lower bound.

Keep a stack of values whose right subtree is still open and a variable low. For each value: if it is below low return false; while the stack top is smaller than the value, pop it and set low to it; then push the value.
editorial: Simulate the construction with a stack that holds the current left spine. When the next value is smaller than the stack top it goes into the left subtree of the top, so just push it. When it is larger, it belongs to the right subtree of the last stack element that is smaller than it: pop all those elements, and remember the last popped one as low. From then on, nothing in the sequence may ever be below low, because that would need to be placed inside a subtree that is already closed.

Every value is pushed and popped at most once, so the algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(n) stack space in the worst case. An alternative is the recursive split 'smaller part, then larger part' which costs O(n log n) on balanced input and O(n^2) on a chain.
